pedagogy.summary: Comparing and ordering fractions with different numerators AND denominators, using either a common denominator (rename both with equivalent fractions, then compare numerators) or benchmark reasoning (is each fraction less than, equal to, or more than 1/2 — or near 0 or 1?). Benchmarks are fast and build number sense; common denominators are general. Conclusions are justified with visual models. This is a known hard skill — on the 2004 NAEP, 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions from least to greatest.
bestPractices: Teach benchmark reasoning with 0, 1/2 and 1: decide which side of 1/2 each fraction sits on (5/8 > 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 < 1/2) (IES Rec 3).
Teach the common-denominator method as renaming both fractions with equivalents, then comparing numerators.
Use minimally-labelled number lines (0, 1/2, 1) for landmark placement, and dual-labelled lines (one unit sequence above, another below) for different denominators (IES Rec 2).
Choose the strategy to fit the numbers — benchmarks when they straddle 1/2, common denominator when they are close.
Justify with a model and guard against whole-number bias.
keyRepresentations: Dual-labelled number line for different denominators
Ratio table / times-tables for the common multiple
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone (3/8 vs 5/12 → '5 > 3 so 5/12 is bigger', or '12 > 8 so smaller') (IES)
Comparing without a common denominator (cross-adding, or comparing tops and bottoms separately)
Renaming only one fraction, or using a non-common multiple

learn.summary: Learners compare and order fractions with different numerators and denominators using two complementary strategies: (1) renaming both fractions to a common denominator and comparing numerators, and (2) benchmark reasoning with 0, 1/2, and 1 (deciding which side of 1/2 each fraction sits on, or whether it is near 0 or 1). Benchmarks are quick and build number sense; common denominators are general-purpose. Conclusions are justified with visual models (partitioned bars, number lines). The core misconception to guard against is whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone. This is a known hard skill: on the 2004 NAEP, 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions from least to greatest.

activities.title: Strategy workbench: common denominator OR benchmark
feedback: If a learner compares numerators and denominators separately or cross-adds, show that only a shared denominator licenses comparing the top numbers — re-partition both bars to the same grid and compare again.

If a learner renames only one fraction or uses a denominator that is not a common multiple of both, point out both fractions must reach the SAME denominator; verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence.
If a learner misplaces a fraction relative to 1/2 (e.g. calls 3/7 more than 1/2), have them compare the numerator to half the denominator: half of 7 is 3.5, and 3 is less than 3.5, so 3/7 < 1/2.
Confirm correct reasoning by asking them to justify with the visual model, not just the final symbols.
activities.rationale: The IES/WWC guide recommends benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 as reference points and number lines (minimally-labelled for landmarks; dual-labelled for different denominators) to support comparison, and names whole-number bias as the core misconception. Offering both renaming and benchmark strategies lets learners pick the efficient method and build general competence.
sourceClaims: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
learnerActions: Take a pair such as 3/8 versus 5/12. Choose the common-denominator path: re-partition both bars (on paper or with a model) to the same fine grid — twenty-fourths — so 3/8 becomes 9/24 and 5/12 becomes 10/24, then compare the numerators 9 versus 10.

Take a pair such as 5/8 versus 3/7. Choose the benchmark path: place each on a number line marked 0, 1/2, 1. Decide which side of 1/2 each sits on (5/8 is more than 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 is less than 1/2 because 3 is less than half of 7).
Switch into an ordering task: drag or write three or more fractions (e.g. 2/3, 3/5, 7/10) onto a line or into order, choosing whichever strategy fits the numbers.
State, for each comparison, which strategy you chose and why it suited those particular numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Renaming two fractions to the same denominator makes them directly comparable (the comparison collapses to comparing numerators), and the 1/2 benchmark settles many comparisons at a glance without full computation. Choosing the strategy to fit the numbers is part of the skill.

activities.title: Dual-labelled and benchmark number lines
feedback: If a learner places a fraction on the wrong side of 1/2, return to comparing the numerator with half the denominator.
If a learner is unsure whether a fraction is near 0 or near 1, check how close the numerator is to 0 or to the denominator (e.g. 1/5 is near 0, 4/5 is near 1).
If a learner struggles to compare across the two denominators, align the two labelled sequences and read off which mark lies further right.
activities.rationale: IES/WWC recommends minimally-labelled number lines for landmark placement and dual-labelled lines for comparing different denominators. A reference line aids recall and placement; note it does not by itself carry out a full ordering or re-partition, so pair it with the active strategies above.
sourceClaims: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
learnerActions: Use a number line marked only 0, 1/2, 1 and place common fractions where they belong relative to those landmarks; for each, say whether it is more than, equal to, or less than one half.
Decide whether 4/9 is more or less than a half by comparing 4 with half of 9 (4.5): 4 is less than 4.5, so 4/9 < 1/2 — no common denominator needed.
Order 1/5, 4/5, 5/9 using only benchmarks: 1/5 sits just above 0, 5/9 is just over 1/2 (5 is more than 4.5), and 4/5 is near 1, giving 1/5 < 5/9 < 4/5.
For two different denominators, use a dual-labelled line (one unit sequence of marks above the line, the other below) to see where each fraction falls and which is larger.
Explain how the landmarks 0, 1/2 and 1 let you decide a comparison without finding a common denominator.
activities.intendedInsight: A number line anchored to 0, 1/2 and 1 gives fractions a magnitude and a 'side of 1/2' (and a sense of nearness to 0 or 1), so many comparisons can be read off directly; dual labelling lets two different denominators be compared on one line.

activities.title: Check and consolidate ordering and benchmark decisions
feedback: If a learner orders by single digits ('7/10 is smallest because 10 is biggest'), rename all three to a common denominator or place them on a 0/½/1 line and compare magnitudes.
If a learner grinds a full common-denominator computation for 5/8 vs 3/7, prompt the quicker 1/2 benchmark.
Reward correct answers that also carry a model-based justification.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fill-in tasks efficiently check whether learners can apply each strategy and avoid whole-number bias, and surface whether a learner works in only one register (benchmark or common denominator). These checks confirm application but do not, on their own, elicit the independent construction that the workbench tasks require.
learnerActions: Order a set such as 2/3, 3/5, 7/10 from smallest to largest and show working (e.g. common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30, giving 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10).
Answer a quick benchmark question: 'Is 5/8 more or less than 1/2?' and justify.
Rename both fractions of a pair to a shared common denominator before comparing, and check the order you get.
Sort a set of fractions into 'less than 1/2' and 'more than 1/2'.
Keep the same-numerator shortcut in play: with equal numerators, the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction (2/3 > 2/5).
Check that a different common denominator does not change the order (e.g. using 60 instead of 30 gives the same ordering).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent comparison means ordering correctly, choosing an efficient strategy, and justifying with a model — not just getting a final symbol right. Any valid common denominator yields the same order.

constraints: Learners must reach fractions with DIFFERENT numerators and denominators; same-denominator or same-numerator pairs alone are stepping stones, not the full objective.
Both strategies should be available: benchmark reasoning when fractions straddle 1/2 or sit near 0 or 1, and common denominators when fractions are close together or benchmarks do not separate them.

A benchmark/reference number line with fractions pre-placed is a recall and placement scaffold; it does not re-partition fractions or carry out an ordering, so it must be combined with active renaming and ordering work.

Recognition-only responses (multiple choice, sorting, fill-in) check application but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a full ordering with justification; include a task where the learner produces the ordering and its reasoning.
Always require justification with a visual model and explicitly guard against whole-number bias (ordering by numerator or denominator alone).
Verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence and ensure both fractions reach the same common multiple.

Comparing a fixed numerator (as in same-numerator pairs) with a fixed denominator varies different quantities; there is no 'denominator rule that flips', so explain each comparison by magnitude rather than a sign-flip rule.

Live re-partitioning of bars to a shared grid and drag-to-order on a line are example interaction mechanisms that make the strategies concrete; they are illustrative, not required mechanisms — the same work can be done with drawn bars and written orderings.

Interpret this content for approximately ages 9–10; in the England curriculum Year 5 pupils compare and order fractions whose denominators are all multiples of the same number, and Year 6 extends this to comparing and ordering fractions more generally, including fractions greater than 1 (source marked unverified).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The IES/WWC claim is marked verified in the source row; the England National Curriculum claim is marked unverified — treat the age/year-stage framing accordingly.
Restored two benchmark-only examples (4/9 vs 1/2; ordering 1/5, 4/5, 5/9) from the original assessment so the 'near 0 or 1' landmarks are actually exercised, not merely asserted.

The consolidation activity's sourceClaims are [] because its rationale concerns recognition-task efficacy, which no source claim directly supports; the IES/WWC claim is retained only on the two activities whose rationales it does support (benchmarks, number lines, whole-number bias).

Non-preferred artefact alternatives (quiz-style checks, reference-only image line, and the noted poor fit of 3D and in-role dialogue for this planar, doing-based task) are preserved as scaffolds/limits rather than as universal pedagogical laws; a sort can check classification into </>1/2 but does not itself elicit a full justified ordering.

probeDeeper: Why does giving both fractions the same denominator let you just compare the top numbers?
Is 4/9 more or less than a half? How can you tell without a common denominator?
You used 30 as the common denominator — could a different common denominator work? Would the order change?
Order these using only benchmarks, no calculation: 1/5, 4/5, 5/9.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10 (common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30). And 5/8 > 3/7, because 5/8 is more than 1/2 (5 is more than half of 8) while 3/7 is less than 1/2 (3 is less than half of 7).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — orders by numerator or denominator alone ('7/10 is smallest because 10 is biggest')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rename all three to a common denominator, or place them on a 0/½/1 line, and compare magnitudes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders without renaming, using single digits

errorPatterns.pattern: Renames only one fraction or uses a non-common denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Both fractions must be renamed to the SAME denominator; verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts one fraction but not the other, or compares over different denominators

errorPatterns.pattern: Benchmark misapplied — 'judges 3/7 to be more than 1/2'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the numerator to half the denominator (half of 7 is 3.5, so 3/7 < 1/2)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts 3/7 on the wrong side of 1/2

responseLevels.gap: Orders by single digits (numerator or denominator); benchmark reasoning absent or wrong.
responseLevels.full: Orders correctly via common denominators (or sound benchmark reasoning) and settles 5/8 vs 3/7 with 1/2 without full computation, justifying both and selecting the efficient strategy for the numbers.
responseLevels.partial: Uses a common denominator correctly for the ordering but cannot apply the 1/2 benchmark efficiently (grinds or errs), or benchmarks but cannot carry out a general common-denominator comparison — works in only one register.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Task: order these three fractions from smallest to largest and show your working — 2/3, 3/5, 7/10. Then use the benchmark 1/2 to decide quickly which is larger: 5/8 or 3/7. I'll watch which methods you use.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who renames to a common denominator (or reasons by benchmarks) orders correctly and settles 5/8 vs 3/7 with 1/2, without full computation. A whole-number-bias child orders by numerators or denominators alone; a child lacking benchmark sense grinds a common denominator for 5/8 vs 3/7 or misjudges which side of 1/2 they fall.
